sleep-protection.text: INTRODUCTION
sleep-protection.html: INTRODUCTION

sleep-protection.text: Sometimes life can hit you real hard, and that can make your day a nightmare, but that doesn’t mean your night has to have them too. For many people, falling asleep can feel very difficult; their minds race with worries, their bodies stay tense, and they replay events from the day, or, for some, painful experiences from the past. If you have ever stayed awake at night feeling exhausted but unable to sleep, or if you wake up feeling unrested, you are not alone. Research shows that about 33% to 50% of adults regularly have trouble falling or staying asleep, and around 7% to 18% meet the criteria for insomnia (Rossman, 2019). For people who have experienced trauma, these numbers are even higher, with 70% to 91% of individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) reporting serious sleep problems (Isaac et al., 2023).

sleep-protection.text: This paper is written for anyone who struggles with sleep, whether you have a diagnosed sleep disorder, have experienced trauma, or simply find that stress affects your ability to rest. It is also intended for practitioners, students, and anyone interested in understanding what research says about non-medication sleep treatments. The main question guiding this review is: What does current research tell us about cognitive behavioural approaches to improving sleep, and how can these findings be turned into practical strategies that are accessible to many people? To answer this, I conducted a narrative review of five peer-reviewed articles published within the last ten years. This paper will walk through those articles in an organized way, moving from the broadest overview of sleep interventions down to the most specific applications, and will end with a practical "Sleep Protection Ritual" that distills the research into a simple, nightly practice.

sleep-protection.text: METHODS
sleep-protection.html: METHODS

sleep-protection.text: My goal for this paper was to create a clear and organized narrative that moves from general ideas to more specific details, helping readers understand both the overall picture and the practical aspects of cognitive behavioural sleep interventions. I started by choosing search terms based on my topic proposal, which focused on trauma-informed sleep strategies. The main search terms included "cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia," "CBT-I," "sleep interventions," "trauma and sleep," "insomnia treatment," and "pediatric insomnia." I also used broader terms like "sleep health promotion" to find review articles that could give a general overview of the field. I mainly searched in PubMed and PsycINFO, since these databases are well known for covering both medical and psychological research. I also used Google Scholar to find more articles and to make sure I did not miss any important studies.

sleep-protection.text: I made sure that the articles were peer-reviewed, written in English, and published within the last ten years (2016–2026). I focused on systematic reviews and meta-analyses because these types of studies provided the strongest evidence about how effective interventions are. I also selected articles that represented different groups (such as general adult populations, people with trauma, and children and adolescents) and different perspectives (such as broad overviews, detailed explanations of CBT-I, and long-term outcome studies). I chose this range on purpose so that the review would reflect the real complexity of sleep problems in everyday life. However, there are a few limitations to my approach. First, because I focused mainly on cognitive behavioural methods, other effective interventions (e.g., mind–body exercise or bright light therapy) are not discussed in detail, even though research shows they can be very effective (Albakri et al., 2021). I also focused more on review articles and meta-analyses rather than individual studies. This allowed me to cover a wider range of research, but it also means that some detailed findings from individual studies may not be fully included.

sleep-protection.text: The five articles were chosen to create a clear and logical flow. The first article (Albakri et al., 2021) is an umbrella review that provides a broad overview of sleep interventions across different populations. The second article (Rossman, 2019) focuses specifically on CBT-I and explains its main components. The third article (van der Zweerde et al., 2019) looks at whether the effects of CBT-I last over time. The fourth article (Isaac et al., 2023) studies CBT-I in adults who have experienced trauma. Finally, the fifth article (Dewald-Kaufmann et al., 2019) looks at children and adolescents, showing that these ideas can be applied across different ages. This structure helps readers see how the fact that CBT-I is effective even when we look at specific groups and longer periods of time.

sleep-protection.text: A Broad View on Sleep Interventions
sleep-protection.html: A Broad View on Sleep Interventions

sleep-protection.text: To understand where cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) fits within the bigger picture, it helps to start with a broad overview. Albakri and colleagues (2021) conducted an umbrella review, which means they reviewed many existing systematic reviews. In total, they looked at 35 reviews and 552 individual studies on non-medication sleep interventions in generally healthy populations. Their goal was to identify what types of interventions exist, who they are designed for, and how effective they are. They grouped these interventions into eleven categories, including sleep education, behaviour change methods, relaxation techniques, physical exercise, mind–body exercise, aromatherapy and massage, environmental changes, psychotherapy, later school start times, and multicomponent approaches.

sleep-protection.text: What makes this review useful is how generalized it is. It shows the many different ways researchers and clinicians have tried to improve sleep, from teaching children about sleep habits to adjusting school schedules to better match adolescents’ natural sleep cycles. Three types of interventions had the strongest evidence: behaviour change methods (especially for infants and young children), and mind–body exercises like yoga and stretching. Other approaches, such as sleep education and relaxation techniques, showed some positive effects as well.

sleep-protection.text: In conclusion, this review shows that sleep interventions are varied and that no single method works for everyone. It also points out that even though many approaches exist, the evidence for some commonly recommended strategies (like sleep education on its own) is mixed. The authors explain that simply giving people information about sleep often does not lead to real behaviour change, and without changing behaviour, sleep is unlikely to improve (Albakri et al., 2021). This is important because it shows that effective sleep interventions need to do more than offer advice; they need to help people actively change the thoughts and behaviours that keep them awake.

sleep-protection.text: Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia
sleep-protection.html: Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia

sleep-protection.text: The next article focuses more closely on CBT-I. Rossman (2019) provides a clear and convincing overview of CBT-I, explaining that it is both highly effective and not used as often as it should be. He reports that CBT-I works just as well as sleep medication, but without side effects, with fewer chances of relapse, and with continued improvement in sleep even after treatment ends.

sleep-protection.text: The article explains CBT-I through five main components. First, sleep consolidation (also known as sleep restriction) involves limiting the time spent in bed to build up the body’s need for sleep, so that when a person goes to bed, they fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer. Second, stimulus control focuses on breaking the association between the bed and being awake. People are told to use the bed only for sleep and sexual activity, and to leave the bedroom if they have not fallen asleep within about 20 minutes. Third, cognitive restructuring helps people recognize and challenge negative thoughts about sleep, such as “I will never fall asleep” or “I will feel terrible tomorrow,” and replace them with more realistic and balanced thoughts. Fourth, sleep hygiene includes habits that support good sleep, such as keeping a regular sleep schedule, avoiding caffeine and alcohol before bed, and limiting screen time in the evening. Finally, relaxation techniques like deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness help calm the body and make it easier to fall asleep.

sleep-protection.text: The Long-Term Effects of CBT-I
sleep-protection.html: The Long-Term Effects of CBT-I

sleep-protection.text: One of the most important things to consider is whether the effects of a treatment lasts over time and if people go back to their old patterns after treatment ends. Van der Zweerde and colleagues (2019) looked at this question by conducting a meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials (RCTs). They studied the long-term effects of CBT-I at three, six, and twelve months after treatment, comparing people who received CBT-I to those in control groups, such as waitlists or minimal interventions.

Van der Zweerde and colleagues (2019) looked at this question by conducting a meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials (RCTs). sleep-protection.text: The results showed that CBT-I does have lasting effects, although these effects decrease somewhat over time. After three months, the improvement in insomnia severity was large. After six months, it was moderate, and after twelve months, it was smaller but still meaningful. Similar results were found for sleep efficiency and the time it takes to fall asleep (van der Zweerde et al., 2019). Therefore, people who received CBT-I were still sleeping better than those who did not receive treatment even a year later, although the difference between the groups became smaller over time.

sleep-protection.text: The authors suggest a few reasons for this decline. Some people in the control group may have eventually looked for treatment on their own, which would reduce the difference between the groups. It is also possible that people who received CBT-I found it hard to maintain the behaviour changes over time, since lifestyle changes can be difficult to stick with. Therefore, the authors conclude that CBT-I leads to meaningful improvements that can last up to a year, supporting its role as a beneficial treatment for insomnia. Lastly, this meta-analysis offers important information to note. First, the skills learned in CBT-I can continue to help for months after treatment ends, but these effects can fade over time, which means that continued practice is important. This supports the idea of having a regular nightly routine, as consistency is important, and the benefits are stronger when the habits become part of everyday life.

sleep-protection.text: Effect of CBT-I on Adults with Trauma Symptoms
sleep-protection.html: Effect of CBT-I on Adults with Trauma Symptoms

sleep-protection.text: For many people, sleep problems are not only caused by stress or poor habits, they are also closely connected to past traumatic experiences. Isaac and colleagues (2023) conducted a systematic review that focused on CBT-based treatments for insomnia and nightmares in adults with trauma symptoms. The authors only included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that used both self-report measures and objective sleep measures, such as actigraphy.

Isaac and colleagues (2023) conducted a systematic review that focused on CBT-based treatments for insomnia and nightmares in adults with trauma symptoms. The authors only included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that used both self-report measures and objective sleep measures, such as actigraphy.

sleep-protection.text: Their findings support the effectiveness of CBT-I for this group. In the five RCTs that they examined, CBT-I, either on its own or combined with nightmare-focused treatments (e.g. imagery rehearsal therapy (IRT) or exposure, relaxation, and rescripting therapy (ERRT)), reduced how often nightmares occurred, with medium to large effects. It also improved sleep efficiency, with effects ranging from small to large. Additionally, better sleep was linked to reductions in PTSD symptoms, even though the treatments were not directly focused on trauma. This suggests that sleep and mental health are strongly connected, as when sleep improves, psychological symptoms improve as well.

For example, actigraphy showed changes in total sleep time, but did not always capture changes in other areas like sleep efficiency. This suggests that objective tools may not fully reflect how people actually experience their sleep. The authors explain that self-report measures may capture emotional aspects of sleep (such as anxiety or feeling on edge) that devices like actigraphy cannot measure. This difference is important because it shows that sleep is not only a biological process but also a personal and subjective experience. For people with trauma, feeling safe at night may matter just as much as how many hours they sleep.

sleep-protection.text: DISCUSSION
sleep-protection.html: DISCUSSION

sleep-protection.text: Taken together, these five articles create a clear and consistent picture. The umbrella review (Albakri et al., 2021) shows that there are many different types of sleep interventions, with strong evidence for several approaches, such as behaviour change methods, and mind–body exercises, relaxation techniques, etc... Rossman (2019) then introduces CBT-I as the leading non-medication treatment for chronic insomnia and explains it through five key components that can be learned and applied. The meta-analysis by Van der Zweerde and colleagues (2019) shows that these benefits are not short-term; they can last for months after treatment, even though they may decrease somewhat over time. Isaac and colleagues (2023) expand this further by showing that CBT-I also helps people who have experienced trauma, reducing both nightmares and PTSD symptoms. Finally, Dewald-Kaufmann and colleagues (2019) show that CBT-I can be adapted for children and adolescents, helping address sleep problems early before they become long-term issues.

They work for healthy adults with mild sleep problems, as well as for those with severe insomnia, trauma backgrounds, or different developmental needs. The main techniques, which are limiting time in bed, challenging unhelpful thoughts, practicing good sleep habits, and using relaxation to calm the body, are consistent across these groups, and this consistency is what makes CBT-I so effective. It provides a set of skills that people can learn and adjust to fit their own situations.

sleep-protection.text: Limitations
sleep-protection.html: Limitations

sleep-protection.text: The research also raises important issues and limitations. One issue is why CBT-I is still not widely used. Rossman (2019) suggests that this is partly due to a lack of trained professionals and the strong influence of medication marketing, but I believe there may also be deeper cultural reasons. Many people may see sleep problems as something that should be treated with medication rather than as something that can be improved through behaviour and skills. Changing this way of thinking will likely require not only better training for clinicians but also more public awareness about how effective non-medication approaches can be.

sleep-protection.text: Another important issue is the difference between subjective and objective measures of sleep, as discussed by Isaac and colleagues (2023). When tools like actigraphy and self-reports give different results, it raises the question of which one we should trust. In my opinion, this difference is not a problem to solve but something researchers should actively work with. Objective measures are useful for tracking physical sleep patterns, while self-reports capture how people actually experience their sleep, including anxiety, frustration, and whether they feel rested. For individuals with trauma, the sense of safety at night may matter more than the amount of sleep. Because of this, I think future studies should consistently use both types of measures together rather than treating one as more valid than the other. It may also be useful to directly examine when and why these measures do not match, as it could reveal important insights about how psychological experiences shape sleep.

sleep-protection.text: Future Directions
sleep-protection.html: Future Directions

sleep-protection.text: Looking ahead, several directions for future research and practice become clear. First, we need more studies that look at the long-term effects of CBT-I beyond one year. Van der Zweerde and colleagues (2019) show that the benefits last up to 12 months, but what happens after two or five years? Understanding these longer-term effects could help researchers create better ways to maintain progress, such as follow-up sessions or ongoing self-monitoring.

sleep-protection.text: Conclusion
sleep-protection.html: Conclusion

sleep-protection.text: For people who struggle with sleep, whether because of stress, trauma, or a diagnosed sleep disorder, the effects can impact every part of life. The research reviewed here strongly supports cognitive behavioural approaches to sleep, especially CBT-I. From the broad overview of the umbrella review to the more focused studies on trauma and younger populations, the evidence consistently shows that these approaches are effective, that their benefits last over time, and that they can be adapted to suit different individuals.

sense-foraging.text: Imagine trying to reason your way out of a feeling that isn’t necessarily coming from your thoughts in the first place. Your chest feels tight, your body heavy, or maybe everything feels strangely numb. Yet, the advice you are given is to “challenge your thoughts” or “reframe your beliefs.” Perhaps you have even been told to simply “think positively!” For many people experiencing depressive or anxious symptoms, distress is not simply something that can be thought away, as the individual may not have the emotional energy and/or cognitive capacity to engage with their internal dialogue. Rather, it is felt in the body, often in ways that make cognitive strategies feel inaccessible. If this is the case, then an important question emerges: what kinds of interventions are actually useful and within reach when thinking itself becomes difficult? Fortunately, approaches that focus on engaging the senses (such as through touch, sound, temperature, or smell) may offer a way of responding to distress that does not require immediate insight or effortful reflection, but instead begins with creating small shifts in the body.

sense-foraging.text: The present narrative review explores sensory self-soothing as an alternative or complementary approach to traditional emotion regulation strategies. sense-foraging.text: Sensory Dysregulation as a Core Part of Emotional Distress
sense-foraging.html: Sensory Dysregulation as a Core Part of Emotional Distress

sense-foraging.text: One of the most consistent findings across recent research is that sensory processing plays a much bigger role in emotional experience than is often acknowledged. Rather than being purely cognitive, depression and anxiety appear to involve disruptions in how individuals experience and respond to sensory input.
sense-foraging.html: One of the most consistent findings across recent research is that sensory processing plays a much bigger role in emotional experience than is often acknowledged. Rather than being purely cognitive, depression and anxiety appear to involve disruptions in how individuals experience and respond to sensory input.

sense-foraging.text: Paquet et al. (2022) provide strong evidence for this by showing that individuals with major depressive disorder tend to exhibit increased sensory sensitivity, greater sensation avoidance, and low registration, along with reduced sensation seeking. These patterns suggest that people with depression may experience their environment in a way that is either overwhelming, under-stimulating, or both at the same time. Importantly, these sensory patterns were linked to symptoms such as anxiety, psychomotor slowing, and low self-esteem, suggesting that they are not just side effects, but meaningfully connected to the disorder itself.

sense-foraging.text: A particularly useful insight from this study is that depression may involve both hypersensitivity and disconnection, where individuals both withdraw from stimulation and struggle to feel engaged with their environment. On one hand, certain stimuli may feel too intense or uncomfortable (such as lights being too bright, noises being too loud, or certain fabrics being irritating), leading to avoidance. On the other hand, individuals may also feel disengaged or numb (in cases like an individual not noticing temperature changes, hunger cues, or even social signals unless they are very intense), reflecting low sensory registration. This helps reframe symptoms like withdrawal and lack of motivation as possible responses to sensory dysregulation, rather than simply cognitive or emotional deficits. Escelsior et al. (2025) extended this idea by showing that similar sensory processing patterns are linked to a range of psychological difficulties, including depression, mania, and psychosis. This suggests that sensory dysregulation may not be specific to one disorder, but instead reflects a broader vulnerability that affects how individuals interact with their environment.

This reinforces the idea that emotional and sensory processes are closely intertwined, rather than separate systems.

sense-foraging.text: Sensory Input as a Way to Regulate Emotion
sense-foraging.html: Sensory Input as a Way to Regulate Emotion

sense-foraging.text: If sensory processing plays a role in emotional distress, it makes sense that it could also be used as a pathway for regulation. Several studies suggest that engaging the senses can directly influence physiological systems involved in stress and emotions. Xie et al. (2025) show that combined tactical (touch) and olfactory (smell) stimulation can reduce anxiety and improve autonomic balance. Tactile stimulation may include experiences such as soft fabrics, gentle pressure, or skin contact with textured materials, while olfactory stimulation may involve exposure to scents such as lavender or other calming aromas. These combined inputs were found to influence physiological markers such as heart rate variability, suggesting a shift toward parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) dominance over a sympathetic (fight-or-flight) state of arousal. What is particularly interesting about this finding is that the effects appear to occur at a physiological level, suggesting that sensory input may help regulate emotional states without requiring cognitive effort.

This suggests that learning to tolerate and observe intense sensory input may help individuals build both physiological and cognitive flexibility and strength. sense-foraging.text: The Role of Environment and Everyday Sensory Experience
sense-foraging.html: The Role of Environment and Everyday Sensory Experience

sense-foraging.text: In addition to structured interventions, everyday sensory experiences also appear to play an important role in shaping emotional states. This shifts the focus from what individuals do intentionally to regulate emotion, to the environments they exist within. For instance, sensory engagement with physical environments has been found to support mindfulness and well-being, suggesting that certain environments may naturally promote calm and reflection (Yurttaş & Altay, 2025). These environments may include natural settings, such as green spaces, water features, or quiet, minimalist interiors that reduce sensory overload while providing gentle, predictable stimulation. Features such as soft lighting, natural materials (like wood or stone), and open space can create a sense of calm and safety, which may support emotional regulation. Similarly, Jiang (2022) demonstrated that natural soundscapes can influence emotional responses and behaviour. A “soundscape” refers to the combination of sounds present in an environment, such as birds chirping, water flowing, wind rustling the leaves on trees, or even distant ambient noise. Exposure to said natural sounds has been associated with more positive emotional states and greater relaxation, compared to artificial or urban noises. This suggests that auditory input alone can shape emotional experience in meaningful, relatively accessible ways.

sense-foraging.html: Practical Applications: Sensory Self-Soothing

sense-foraging.text: The above ideas have begun to translate into practical strategies that are being further researched and validated day-by-day. Sokmen and Watters (2016) describe the use of personalized self-soothing kits, which may include items such as weighted objects or soft fabrics for touch, scented lotions for smell, calming music for auditory input, and visual items such as photographs or lighting tools. Temperature-based items (such as heat packs or cooling clothes) may also be included. However, the main key feature of these kits is personalization, because what is calming for one person may be irritating or overwhelming for another. These kits are designed to provide accessible and flexible tools for managing emotional distress or discomfort.

sense-foraging.text: Discussion
sense-foraging.html: Discussion

sense-foraging.text: Overall, current research suggests that sensory self-soothing is a promising approach to emotion regulation, particularly in situations where cognitive strategies of “thinking differently” or “thinking more positively” are difficult to access or use. By working through the body’s senses via a bottom-up approach, these strategies may provide a more accessible form of relief when it comes to managing emotional distress.

sense-foraging.text: At the same time, the effectiveness of these approaches depends on several important factors. One of the most important is individual differences. As highlighted by Paquet et al. (2022), people vary widely in how they process sensory input, which means that one strategy should not be viewed as a one-size-fits-all solution. Individuals may differ in their sensory thresholds (how much input someone needs to notice a stimulus), and behavioural response (whether they seek or avoid stimulation). For example, someone with high sensory sensitivity may find scents or textures overwhelming and aversive, while someone with low registration may need strong input (such as colder water or louder soundscapes) to experience any effect at all. This truly highlights the importance of the personalization of treatment when it comes to actively engaging in your senses with the aim of improving your mental wellbeing.

sense-foraging.text: Conclusion and Future Directions
sense-foraging.html: Conclusion and Future Directions

sense-foraging.text: Sensory self-soothing represents a meaningful shift toward understanding emotional regulation as an embodied process. By focusing on sensory and physiological experiences, these strategies offer an alternative way of supporting individuals during moments when cognitive approaches may not be accessible. However, this approach is not a universal solution. Its effectiveness heavily depends on individual differences and how it is used. Future research should focus on identifying who benefits most from sensory-based interventions, and specific ways in how these strategies can support, rather than replace, emotional processing.

restored-spirits.html: INTRODUCTION

restored-spirits.text: There is a moment that happens in kitchens that is easy to overlook. Someone is chopping vegetables, another is stirring something on the stove, and conversation fills the space in between. Nothing about it feels clinical or intentional, yet people often leave these moments feeling lighter, more connected, and somehow better than before. In contrast, eating alone or rushing through a meal rarely creates the same effect. At a time when loneliness and mental health concerns are increasing, it is worth asking whether these small, everyday experiences, like cooking with others, play a larger role in wellbeing than we tend to recognize. While traditional mental health treatments often focus on therapy or medication, there has been a growing interest in behavioural strategies. Everyday activities that can improve mental health in a more accessible and engaging way. Cooking is one of those activities that has recently gained attention in both research and clinical settings; rather than being viewed only as a life skill, cooking is now being explored as a meaningful intervention that can improve mood, increase self-efficacy, and promote social connection.

restored-spirits.html: METHOD

restored-spirits.text: This narrative review examine’s current research on cooking as a behavioural strategy for improving mental health and well-being. Studies were selected across both clinical and non-clinical populations to allow for comparison between structured therapeutic applications of cooking and its effects in everyday contexts. Relevant articles were identified using academic databases including PubMed, Google Scholar, and PsycINFO. Search terms included combinations of “cooking interventions,” “culinary therapy,” “mental health,” “wellbeing,” “social eating,” “group cooking”, “depression,” and “prosocial behaviour.” These terms were selected to capture both clinical and everyday contexts in which cooking may influence mental health. The selection criteria focused on peer-reviewed articles published within the past 10 years, with an emphasis on studies that examined psychological outcomes such as mood, emotional well-being, social connection, and quality of life. Both experimental studies and review articles were included in order to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the topic. In addition, one paper on social eating was included to provide a theoretical framework for understanding the role of shared experiences in enhancing well-being. Cooking may also involve elements of mindfulness, since it requires focusing on what is happening in the moment, such as smells, textures, and changes in food. This may help explain its positive effects on mental well-being.

restored-spirits.text: Cooking as a Mental Health Intervention
restored-spirits.html: Cooking as a Mental Health Intervention

restored-spirits.text: A growing body of research suggests that cooking interventions can have meaningful effects on psychological well-being. One of the most significant examinations of this topic comes from a systematic review by Farmer et al. (2018), which analyzed multiple studies on cooking programs, including group-based classes, community workshops, and therapeutic interventions, and their psychosocial outcomes. The review found that cooking interventions are generally associated with improvements in self-esteem, socialization, and overall quality of life. These findings are important because they show that cooking is not just beneficial for physical health, but also has measurable psychological effects. However, Farmer et al. also highlight an important limitation, which is that much of the existing research lacks strong methods, with small sample sizes and non-randomized designs. This suggests that while the findings are promising, they should be interpreted with some caution. Despite these limitations, the consistency of positive outcomes across studies indicates that cooking is likely to play a meaningful role in improving wellbeing.

restored-spirits.html: Cooking as a Social and Prosocial Activity

restored-spirits.text: While existing research supports the idea that cooking can improve mental health, a closer look at more recent studies suggests that these benefits may be significantly influenced by the social context in which cooking takes place. Rather than being purely an individual activity, cooking often involves preparing food for others, working collaboratively, or sharing the final product. This raises the possibility that the psychological benefits of cooking are not only tied to the activity itself but also to its role as a prosocial and interactive behaviour. One study that directly addresses this idea is the work by Hui et al. (2026), which examines the psychological effects of prosocial cooking, in simpler terms, cooking for others. Across multiple studies, the authors found that individuals reported higher levels of positive affect and subjective happiness when they engaged in cooking for someone else, compared to cooking for themselves. Interestingly, these benefits were most consistently observed at the momentary level, meaning that people felt better during or immediately after the act of cooking for others. This suggests that the emotional rewards of cooking may be closely tied to the intention behind the activity, rather than the activity alone.

restored-spirits.text: The Role of Shared Eating in Enhancing Psychological Reward
restored-spirits.html: The Role of Shared Eating in Enhancing Psychological Reward

restored-spirits.text: To understand why cooking with others may be particularly beneficial, it is important to examine research on shared eating experiences. While cooking is the process, eating is often the outcome, and both are closely connected. Studies on social eating provide insight into the psychological and even biological mechanisms that make shared food experiences especially rewarding. One study by Huang et al. (2022) explored how the idea of eating together influences both subjective experience and brain activity. Participants were shown images of food labelled either as “eating together” or “eating alone,” and were asked to rate how enjoyable the food appeared. The results showed that foods associated with eating together were consistently rated as more pleasant and desirable. In addition, the eating together condition was associated with increased activation in brain regions linked to reward processing, particularly the insula. These findings suggest that the social context of eating can directly influence how rewarding an experience feels, even at a neural level. In other words, the presence of others enhances not only the emotional experience of eating, but also the brain’s response to it. This provides a biological explanation for why shared meals often feel more enjoyable and meaningful than eating alone.

restored-spirits.text: Strengths and Limitations
restored-spirits.html: Strengths and Limitations

restored-spirits.text: While the research reviewed in this paper presents a strong case for cooking as a beneficial behavioural strategy, several important questions and limitations remain. One of the most consistent issues across studies is the lack of methodological accuracy, particularly in intervention-based research. As noted by Farmer et al. (2018), many cooking studies rely on small sample sizes, lack control groups, or use self-reported measures of well-being. This makes it difficult to determine the extent to which observed improvements are directly caused by cooking, rather than other factors such as social interaction or increased attention from researchers. Another limitation is the difficulty in separating the effects of cooking itself from the social context in which it occurs. Many of the most positive findings come from group-based or prosocial cooking situations, which makes it unclear whether cooking alone would produce the same benefits. This raises an important concern about how cooking is truly an effective intervention, or is it simply a convenient way to facilitate social interaction?

restored-spirits.text: Overall, the evidence reviewed in this paper suggests that cooking is a promising behavioural strategy for improving mental well-being, particularly when it is experienced as a shared activity. Cooking interventions have been shown to improve mood, self-esteem, and quality of life, while prosocial and group-based cooking experiences further enhance these benefits through increased social interaction and emotional connection. Research on shared eating provides additional insight into why these effects occur, showing that social contexts can enhance both the subjective and neural experience of food-related activities. Together, these findings support the idea that cooking is most effective when it is not done alone, but as part of a shared experience that fosters connection and engagement.

sleeping-spell.text: Inadequate sleep is not merely a nocturnal inconvenience; it is a profound disruptor of physiological homeostasis, metabolic function, and long-term psychological resilience. While pharmacological interventions can offer some amount of relief, they are frequently limited by risks of tolerance and residual daytime sedation upon discontinuation. When movement is linked with pressure, performance, or irrational expectations, it can become something that is avoided rather than utilized as a form of encouragement and support. Conversely, when movement is perceived as something that is adaptable, achievable, and responsive to one’s present state, it may start to operate differently. Meaning, it will no longer be regarded as a demand but as a resource. This transformation in perspective opens up the possibility that exercise does not need to be intense to be impactful, but can instead be small-scale, frequent, and supportive of mental well-being.

steady-motion.text: The first article selected was by Chekroud et al. (2018), who conducted a large cross-sectional study using data from over 1.2 million adults in the United States to assess the relationship between physical activity and mental health. Their results indicate that participants who partook in physical activity reported significantly fewer days of poor mental health in contrast to those who did not exercise, with an average decrease of 1.49 days of poor mental health per month. This decrease correlates to a 43.2% decrease in mental health burden compared to inactive participants, suggesting a significant overall impact. Notably, the study controlled for a broad range of demographic and health-related variables such as age, race, gender, marital status, income, education, body-mass index, physical health status, and prior depression diagnosis, which reinforces belief that the perceived relationship is not simply due to confounding variables. The large sample size and range of controls make the results specifically strong and generalizable.

steady-motion.text: Beyond overall associations, Chekroud et al. (2018) looked at differences across various forms of physical activity and found that all types of exercise were associated with improved mental health outcomes, with reductions ranging from about 11.8% to 22.3% depending on the type of activity. For example, team sports were linked with the largest reductions (22.3% lower), followed by cycling (21.6% lower), and aerobic and gym exercise (20.1% lower), although walking and household activities also displayed clear advantages. The study also discovered a non-linear relationship between exercise and mental health, where moderate levels of activity generated the best improvements. The lowest mental health burden was linked with exercise sessions of about 45 minutes, taking place three to five times per week. However, exercise sessions that were less than 45 minutes or more than 60 minutes were linked with worse mental health results. These findings indicate that both the type and dose of activity are important, but that moderate, frequent engagement is the most impactful for mental health.

(2022) utilized a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies to assess how physical activity predicts the future development of depression over time, allowing for more robust temporal conclusions than cross-sectional research. Their results showed an inverse curvilinear dose-response relationship, meaning that the biggest decreases in depression risk take place when people move away from total inactivity to even small amounts of exercise. Individuals who completed half the recommended level of activity had an 18% lower risk of depression, while those completing the full recommended levels had a 25% lower risk. This suggests that a significant part of the mental health benefit occurs at also relatively low amounts of activity.

This supports the idea that the most effective change is simply shifting away from inactivity. Since the analysis centered on incident depression across follow-up periods ranging over several years, it contributes robust evidence that physical activity plays a significant role in prevention instead of the reduction of symptoms only. For example, if less physically active adults had successfully fulfilled the present exercise recommendations, then 11.5% of cases of depression could have been avoided. Overall, the results emphasize that even small, attainable increases in movement can significantly modify mental health risk.

steady-motion.text: While the evidence supporting exercise as a mental health intervention is convincing, it raises vital questions about how and why it works, and how it should be practically applied. One critical issue is the difference between correlation and causation. Although research such as Wanjau et al. (2023) indicates a probable causal relationship, most of the existing evidence continues to be observational, making it hard to completely rule out other plausible explanations. For instance, individuals with enhanced baseline mental health may be more likely to participate in exercise, suggesting a bidirectional relationship. Therefore, this creates some uncertainty in placing exercise as a key intervention rather than a complementary one. At the same time, there seems to be a significant disconnect between public perception and the supporting evidence. Physical activity is usually culturally framed as intense, challenging, or discipline-driven, whereas the literature typically shows that moderate and even low levels of activity generate significant benefits. In this regard, the problem is not overhype, but rather misrepresentation, where the positive effects of exercise may be downplayed because it is framed in ways that appear inaccessible or unmanageable.

This goes against the assumption that change must be demanding or extreme and instead suggests that well-being can come from simple, consistent actions. However, a number of vital concerns still remain. It is still unclear how these results generalize across populations, specifically for those with more severe mental health disorders, physical restrictions, or socioeconomic limitations that restrict access to secure or regular movement. Compliance also remains a key challenge, since the impactfulness of exercise relies on continuous participation over time, which many people struggle to maintain. These limitations suggest that the success of physical activity as a treatment may depend less on its efficacy in controlled settings and more on how it is established in everyday life. Regardless of these concerns, the overall promise of this approach is significant and difficult to ignore. This is because, at the end of the day, exercise can be inexpensive, is generally accessible, and is linked with both physical and psychological advantages, making it a uniquely scalable intervention. metaphor-mirror.text: Mental health and wellbeing of young people has become a severe concern in recent decades, as many young individuals are struggling to access safe mental health services (McGorry et al., 2025). Barriers such as lack of supportive community circles, being unaware of the services available, mistrust in these services, fears about the consequences of seeking help, and misconceptions surrounding mental health have largely contributed to this (Drissi El-Bouzaidi, 2015; King, 2019; McGorry et al., 2025). These issues are clearly demonstrated in university student populations, as students have consistently been found to have significantly higher distress levels and worse emotional health when compared to the general population (Linden & Stewart, 2020). This is an issue which clearly affects the University of Toronto (UofT) community, as it is not uncommon to hear UofT being referred to as “UofTears” (Aska, 2023; Villar, 2023). The mental health services at UofT have been extensively criticised (not only by students, but by the Ontario Human Rights Commission) due to many students facing difficulties and consequences when attempting to access adequate and timely mental health support (Mancini & Roumeliotis, 2019; King, 2019; Drissi El-Bouzaidi, 2015; Mandhane, 2018). As such, many students are left to cope with this stress on their own without adequate resources or psychoeducation to do so. Providing students who are in need of support with accessible and realistic self-guided strategies for the prevention of mental health struggles must be developed and disseminated to alleviate some of this distress whenever possible.

metaphor-mirror.text: One technique which may help promote mental health and emotional wellbeing in these student populations is self-guided metaphorical cognitive restructuring (sg-M-CR). This technique is based on traditional cognitive restructuring (CR) used in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) practices, with integration of metaphorical language. Both this technique and self-guided therapeutic practices are growing areas of interest in research, as both can play crucial roles in filling the gaps which are seen in formal therapeutic practices. Sg-M-CR is a promising technique for promoting insight and distress reduction without emotional disruption when reframing maladaptive cognitive thought patterns by strengthening memory connections, integrating abstract and concrete concepts, improving flexible cognitive capabilities, and incorporating vivid imagery.

metaphor-mirror.text: Papers were chosen based on relevancy to the topic, specific focus and purpose (as it is important to include sources which both replicate and expand on previous findings), clarity and validity of methodology used, and significance of findings. These were organized to create a narrative structure by first providing a strong literature base which validated the processes and functions which make M-CR effective, followed by literature which integrated various self-guided practices as a means of investigating the possibility of adapting this technique into a self-guided structure. The first paper by Yu and Colleagues (2025) outlined the underlying neural mechanisms which allow for sg-M-CR to be effective. This was followed by a study conducted by Zhang and colleagues (2023), who focused on the effects of M-CR on distress relief and improvement in wellbeing. This study also used neuroimaging, which allowed for validation of the first study. This was followed by review of a study conducted by Hu and colleagues (2023), which specifically examined the efficacy of M-CR for at-risk nonclinical populations. All of these experiments used paradigms which were brief session periods and were largely self-guided. To further evaluate the presence and use of metaphors in clinical populations, a study by Malkomsen and colleagues (2021) was examined. This study not only gave further information about how metaphors themselves were used by individuals, but also gave a clearer understanding of the subjective experiences of the participants. Lastly, a paper by Pavani and colleagues (2020) was used as a strong source to understand the efficacy and process of translating specific CBT techniques into self-guided practices. Although this paper did not focus specifically on metaphor use in CR, its adaptation of multiple techniques from CBT provide evidence for the possibility of constructing a self-guided intervention.

metaphor-mirror.text: In traditional CR practices, CR aims to promote realistic thinking by restructuring an individual’s thoughts, appraisals, and beliefs (Tolin, 2024). To do this, the individual must first understand what is wrong with their current thought patterns, then reach, accept, and rehearse a way of thinking which is more adaptive. Recognizing that current thoughts are maladaptive can provoke negative self-evaluations and distress, as these distorted or maladaptive cognitive responses that are being analyzed may be seen through this same lens. CR requires a sensitive and informed approach applied consistently and frequently across an extended period of time to mitigate the risk of an individual falling back into negative thought loops and prevent exacerbation of maladaptive self-criticism (Tolin, 2024). As the individual’s maladaptive thought pattern is the target for intervention, directly addressing this belief and recognizing the role it plays in perpetuating maladaptive behaviors and subjective distress can be overwhelming to the individual, as these thought patterns are inherently linked to their sense of self-concept (Tolin, 2024). This may also contribute to a difficulty in identifying and labelling the emotions associated with these maladaptive thought patterns and their consequences.

metaphor-mirror.text: A metaphor is a fundamental concept in language where one scenario or phenomenon is used to represent a different one. Metaphors are most commonly used in order to materialize an abstract concept by using a concrete reference point (Smith, 2008). This allows for a connection to be made between perception, cognition, and behavior; in short, metaphors are the essential building blocks used to construct our understandings of both ourselves and the world around us (Smith, 2008). Metaphors are especially useful tools in communicating feelings, as they are known to stimulate imagination, listener interest, and motivation (Yu et al., 2022). This is especially true in the case of novel metaphors, as the new point of reference offers the opportunity for feelings to be reframed through a new lens (Hartung et al., 2020).

Use of metaphors in the practice of psychotherapy has consistently been found to be beneficial in assisting patients with reframing problems, generating new solutions, and reinforcing adaptive cognition patterns.

metaphor-mirror.text: A study conducted by Yu and colleagues (2025) aimed to investigate the effect of therapeutic metaphors on memory systems. Metaphorical micro-counseling dialogs were used to present scenarios to healthy participants, whose results were measured both through memory tests and with use of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). In this study, participants were first instructed to read a mental distress problem (eg. “I have no motivation to do anything before I get the result of an important exam”) which was followed by either a literal solution (eg. “Live your life with your normal rhythm, thus you will not feel confused”) or metaphorical solution (eg. “Life is like riding a bike, you must keep moving to keep your balance”). During this stage (encoding), participants underwent fMRI to detect brain activity. Then, participants were given four theme words, one of which reflected the typical event which took place in the original problem (eg. appreciation, examination, desire, separation, with examination being the target or correct theme word). During each trial, participants underwent the encoding phase (reading distress problem, reading solution) while imagining themselves vividly as a client in a counselling session for the scenario. During the test phase, the participants were given a solution which was judged as being old or new. If it was judged as old, they were then shown the four theme words and were instructed to choose the target (correct) theme word for the problem.

metaphor-mirror.text: Participants were then divided into three groups: a control group, literal group, and metaphorical group. During the intervention, the participants in the metaphorical group were asked to imagine metaphorical stories which reflected their anxiety. For example, the participants were told to imagine a balloon being inflated in front of their face. The participants were told that in this scenario, there is no escape route and they have no way to know when the balloon will pop. After visualizing the metaphorical scenario, the participants were instructed to relate the metaphorical scenario to their own experiences with anxiety and to write a self-reflection. In this metaphorical story, the balloon is meant to represent the individual’s anxiety, as anxiety is characterized by tense physical states, worried thoughts, and a felt experience of having little control over the worry experienced. The literal group received a straightforward explanation of the characteristics of anxiety, which included typical behaviors, emotions, and thought patterns associated with having an anxiety disorder. Just as the metaphorical group was instructed, the literal group was then asked to relate the explanation to their own experiences with anxiety and to write a self-reflection. Each group participated in four weekly sessions, with each session lasting one hour; in the sessions, metaphorical stories were provided to the metaphorical group, with the literal group receiving the equivalent number of literal explanations. Each session was preceded and followed by a singular nine-point item questionnaire that asked about the individual’s current anxiety level. After the intervention, participants from the groups were asked to recall four of the session topics via a free recall task, and retook the questionnaire assessments.

metaphor-mirror.text: These findings support the idea that M-CR techniques can effectively be used as a method of promoting overall wellness through reducing distress and increasing insightfulness. However, the previous studies primarily used non-clinical populations whose symptoms did not meet the full criteria to indicate a mental disorder diagnosis. As well, these studies did not examine participants’ subjective experiences when responding to metaphor usage. Malkomsen and colleagues (2021) focused their research on a sample of individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) and used semi-structured interviews to examine the qualitative, subjective experiences of these participants. The participants of this study received either psychodynamic (28 sessions) or CBT (16 sessions, with one monthly booster session for three months). The participants underwent clinical assessments at baseline, during the therapy period, at the end, and at follow up sessions one and three years afterwards. After the patients had completed the therapy treatment, they were interviewed with a focus on their experiences with the treatment, their view of the process, and the effects the process had on their relationships and everyday life. The interviews in the study did not solely focus on use of metaphors, but rather aimed to obtain a holistic insight on patient experience. Within these interviews, it was found that patients frequently used specific categories of metaphors to describe the therapeutic process, therapeutic relationship, and symptom improvement. For the therapeutic process, patients often used conceptual metaphors pertaining to surface and depth (e.g. “Digging down), tools (e.g. “get tools” or “build myself up”), sorting and organizing (e.g. “picking up pieces”), and cleaning and emptying (e.g. “sweep the dirt”). When describing the therapeutic relationship, patients often used metaphors based on openness (e.g. “being closed off”), chemistry (e.g. “good chemistry”), and temperature (e.g. “warm therapist” or “cold therapist”). Lastly, patients tended to describe symptom improvement through metaphors such as disease (e.g. “the disease talking”), opponent (e.g. “monsters inside me”), stuck and loosened (e.g. “being stuck”), up and down (e.g. “reduced the fall’), and darkness and light (e.g. “everything is dark”).

metaphor-mirror.text: Malkomsen and colleagues (2021) used these insights to investigate underlying meanings behind these metaphor categories and provide direction for how these metaphors can be interpreted and built upon. This article highlights that the metaphorical categories of using “tools” should often be elaborated on as to allow the patient to gain a deeper understanding into what the specific “tools”, or coping mechanisms, are and why they work for the individual. It is hypothesized that these elaborations will improve patient satisfaction and insight in the therapeutic process. As well, the authors advise that metaphor categories in which patients liken their symptoms to being a “disease” or “opponent” can have both positive and negative effects. These metaphors can motivate the individual to “fight” more to reduce their symptoms, but may also inadvertently result in increased hostility directed towards themself. As well, framing symptoms or problems as an opponent which must be battled can lead to suppression of emotions and thoughts, which can be counterproductive in developing adaptive thought patterns. These insights emphasize the importance of metaphor use when expressing thoughts and emotions, and highlights the effects that specific themes included in metaphors may promote alteration of cognitive thought patterns. As well, this study provides a more nuanced look into individual experience and can be used to inform the example metaphor solutions given to individuals who use sg-M-CR.

metaphor-mirror.text: The first week focused on promoting functional analysis skills. Activities helped participants explore and perceive the relationship between engagement and subjective wellbeing, investigate the causal relationship between thoughts and emotions, increase awareness of different types of negative emotions, and identify the frequencies and coincidences between negative emotions, automatic negative thoughts, and situations in their lives. Week two of the intervention focused primarily on reappraisal of negative automatic thoughts. Activities explored this through relaxation breathing exercises, questioning of their automatic negative thought patterns, seeking evidence for and against these thoughts, and strengthening mental shortcuts for challenging negative thoughts.Week three of the interventions aimed to develop behavioral skills. This was done through activities including relaxation techniques based on imagery, and identification and solving an external problem of theirs. Week four focused on restructuring negative core beliefs. These activities encouraged participants to identify the main rules they follow and the recurring or redundant themes present in their negative automatic thoughts as a way to uncover their negative core beliefs. Activities emphasized challenging core beliefs via reflecting on its development.

This concern may be mitigated by giving the individuals clear instructions for the exercise with sufficient examples, which may be supplemented with a dissection of how these examples are effective. metaphor-mirror.text: Although the evidence base for this mode of application is under-researched, M-CR is a promising technique for promoting mental health. M-CR is effective when used in traditional CBT practices, and additional studies have found that similar self-guided techniques demonstrate small to medium effect sizes (Pavani et al., 2020). Although the application of sg-M-CR may not prove to be a “cure-all”, it may serve as an effective supplementary practice which can be easily incorporated into an everyday routine. There is a clear benefit to this technique in the fact that effects will likely be seen quickly, which may encourage repeated use in the future. As with every health-promoting lifestyle change, it is important to emphasize how repeated practice may strengthen the effects of sg-M-CR. By providing users with a realistic look at what they should expect to see from application of the technique, they may be encouraged to continue use consistently.

nap-spell.text: In the middle of December exam season, it’s 2 p.m. Your notes are beginning to blur, your concentration is fading, and brain fog is starting to set in. You face a familiar choice: do you take a nap or reach for another cup of coffee? For many students, the answer is caffeine, even when it no longer improves focus and instead increases anxiety. Yet a nap may be one of the simplest and most effective low-cost strategies for improving mood, reducing stress, and supporting learning (Friedrich & Schlarb, 2018). This issue matters because university students are routinely expected to perform at a high level while sleep deprived. The value of napping extends beyond students to other high-demand groups, including working adults. Yet a nap is often stigmatised as laziness or poor productivity (Alger et al., 2019; Autumn et al., 2016). In a culture that increasingly normalises exhaustion and chronic sleep loss, practical and accessible forms of rest deserve greater attention (Autumn et al., 2016). Some organisations have already recognised this by incorporating nap spaces to support performance and productivity, suggesting that rest can be treated as a resource rather than a weakness. Given the high levels of stress, fatigue, and sleep disruption experienced by university students, it is important to examine whether daytime naps offer a meaningful way to support both academic functioning and wellbeing. This narrative review argues that naps can be beneficial for university students, particularly during stressful periods, because they may improve mood, support learning, and reduce the cognitive costs of sleep loss, although their effects appear to depend on factors such as duration, frequency, and context.

nap-spell.text: Method
nap-spell.html: Method

nap-spell.text: This narrative review was conducted using Google Scholar to identify recent academic literature on napping and university students. Searches were mostly limited to studies published from 2016 onwards, with a particular focus on peer-reviewed search. Initial search terms included combinations such as ("daytime nap" OR napping OR "power nap") AND ("university student*" OR "college student*" OR "young adult*")* AND ("nap intervention" OR "planned nap") AND (sleep deprivation OR sleep restriction). As patterns in the literature started to emerge, additional searches targeted specific themes, including memory, learning, attention, mood, stress and mental health. As difficulty falling asleep is also relevant to student napping behaviour, further searches examined sleep onset latency and practical strategies that may support it, including kiwifruit, mindfulness, and to-do-list creation. Sources were selected based on relevance to the topic and applicability to napping, as well as university students or similar populations. The papers were organised thematically to develop the narrative of the review, with sections focusing on the benefits of napping, their effects on mood and wellbeing, the role of nap duration and context, as well as barriers to napping.

nap-spell.html: Benefits of napping

nap-spell.text: Memory
nap-spell.html: Memory

nap-spell.text: Given memory’s central role in academic success, it is important to evaluate whether daytime napping supports learning more effectively than simply continuing to study. Cousins et al. (2019b) addressed this directly comparing a nap condition, a cramming condition and a wake-break condition in undergraduate students. Although both the nap and cramming groups demonstrated improved short-term retention relative to the wake-break condition, only the nap group retained a significant memory benefit one week later (d = 0.56). This suggests that napping may strengthen long-term consolidation in a way that cramming does not. Notably, the nap group also reported lower subjective sleepiness during subsequent learning blocks, indicating that the benefits extended beyond retention to support continued encoding capacity. However, the study’s external validity is limited by its use of controlled learning tasks on relatively unengaging topics, rather than the complex course material students usually study. Despite this, its direct comparison of napping and cramming is a meaningful strength, as it reflects a common student tendency to prioritise continued studying over rest.

nap-spell.text: At the neuroimaging level, a separate fMRI study began to explain the mechanistic basis of these behavioural findings. Brain regions implicated in attention and executive control, including the cerebellum, insula, and thalamus, showed reduced activation following sleep deprivation, corresponding with slower reaction times and lower accuracy (Ouyang et al., 2025). Following the nap, activation in these regions rebounded, with increased right insula activation associated with improved reaction time (r = .38, p < .005), suggesting that napping may restore the neural substrates of working memory rather than simply alleviating subjective fatigue. The study's reliance on a sample of young male students limits the generalisability of these findings to the broader student population; however, its within-subject design, (in which each participant completed all three experimental conditions) substantially reduced the influence of individual differences and strengthens confidence in the observed effects.

nap-spell.text: These findings raise a related question: napping may restore what has been lost to sleep deprivation, but can it also protect the capacity to learn new material later in the day? Evidence suggests it can. In adolescents experiencing sleep deprivation, a split sleep schedule incorporating a daytime nap produced better afternoon performance on picture recognition (d = 0.66, p = .015) and factual learning tasks than a continuous sleep schedule, despite equivalent total sleep opportunity (Cousins et al., 2019a). Notably, the benefit was selective to later learning and did not come at the expense of morning performance, suggesting that napping may help restore encoding capacity as homeostatic sleep pressure accumulates across the day. This has direct relevance for students who continue attending lectures and studying well into periods of significant fatigue. The sample’s age range limits how directly these findings transfer to university students, whose academic demands and stressors often differ from those of adolescents (e.g., financial pressure, independent living, and post-secondary workload) (Moore et al., 2021). Nonetheless, the broader implication is meaningful; napping may protect not only what has already been learned, but also the brain's capacity to keep learning effectively.

nap-spell.text: Mental health
nap-spell.html: Mental health

nap-spell.text: While much of the napping literature focuses on cognition, some evidence suggests that naps may also provide short-term emotional benefits during acute stressors. In adults who were not sleep deprived, both a 40-minute daytime nap and wake-break groups lower perceived stress and improved working memory after rest (Wofford et al., 2022). However, only the daytime nap was associated with a reduction in negative affect following the acute psychosocial stressor (t(28) = 2.85, p = .008, d = 0.53). These findings suggest that napping may offer an affective benefit that extends beyond the general relief of simply stepping away from a task. For university students, this is especially relevant, as exam periods, presentations, and deadlines often produce brief but intense episodes of distress that can interfere with functioning even when cognitive performance remains relatively intact. At the same time, the findings should be interpreted cautiously, as the participants were not sleep deprived, whereas insufficient sleep is common in undergraduate populations (Gardani et al., 2022). Nevertheless, the study is valuable in suggesting that naps may help students not only think more clearly, but also recover emotionally during stressful periods.

nap-spell.text: At the same time, the relationship between napping and mental health should not be treated as straightforwardly positive. A two-study investigation of U.S. undergraduates offers a useful corrective by distinguishing between the desire to nap and napping itself (Ostrow et al., 2024). The first study found that napping on the same day was significantly associated with depressed mood, but not anxious mood. A larger follow-up study that controlled for age, gender, and restedness found that nap desire, rather than nap behaviour, predicted both anxious (F(1, 1291) = 6.86, p = .009, partial η² = .005) and depressed mood (F(1, 1291) = 13.46, p < .001, partial η² = .010). This suggests that the urge to nap may sometimes function less as a cause of distress than as a marker of underlying fatigue, low mood, or emotional strain. Napping is therefore best understood not as uniformly beneficial or harmful, but as a behaviour whose meaning depends on context, motivation, and the individual’s broader emotional state.

nap-spell.text: How to Nap Effectively
nap-spell.html: How to Nap Effectively

nap-spell.text: Despite the beneficial evidence regarding napping, it remains underutilised, in part due to its benefits not always experienced consistently. One commonly cited barrier is sleep inertia, the period of grogginess and reduced cognitive performance that can follow waking (Hilditch et al., 2017). This temporary impairment is not trivial; it has been associated with real-world adverse events and safety incidents. For students weighing whether to nap between classes or before an exam, the risk of waking up feeling worse is a reasonable concern. This raises the question of under what conditions does napping produce benefits rather than costs?

nap-spell.text: Several factors appear to worsen sleep inertia, including waking during the circadian low in alertness, prior sleep loss, prolonged wakefulness before sleep, and waking from deeper stages of sleep, particularly slow-wave sleep (Hilditch et al., 2017). For most university students, this points toward short naps of approximately 20 to 30 minutes as the most practical general recommendation. Brief naps appear especially effective when the goal is to improve alertness, mood, and cognitive functioning (Shadab et al., 2026). This is consistent with cross-sectional evidence finding that university students who napped for shorter durations showed better sleep quality, lower stress, and shorter sleep latency, suggesting that briefer naps may reflect a more adaptive pattern overall (Ferreira et al., 2026). At the broader level, a comprehensive umbrella review concluded that naps under 60 minutes were associated with better cognitive performance (SMD = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.37–1.00) and lower fatigue (SMD = −0.76, 95% CI: −1.24 to −0.28), while avoiding many drawbacks linked to longer daytime sleep (Du et al., 2026). These effect sizes were drawn from physically active populations, so their direct applicability to student samples warrants some caution. Taken together, the findings suggest that short naps may be the most useful everyday strategy for students who need a brief period of recovery between classes, study sessions, or stressful academic tasks.

nap-spell.text: Longer naps may still be useful, but their utility appears to be more situational and comes with meaningful trade-offs. Under conditions of heavier fatigue, there is some evidence that longer sleep periods produce stronger restorative effects. For instance, a 90-minute nap outperformed a 40-minute nap on measures of attention (Δ = +3, ηp² = 0.86), perceived recovery (Δ = +0.6, p = 0.02), and mood in an athletic context (Boukhris et al., 2020). Similarly, a 120-minute nap sustained early morning performance better than a 60-minute nap among night-shift workers (Kubo et al., 2007). This suggests that longer naps may be particularly valuable when substantial sleep debt has accumulated. For students facing exam periods or extended sleep disruption, this may have some relevance, though the occupational contexts of both studies mean the findings don’t transfer straightforwardly.

Likewise, long naps have been associated with poorer long-term health outcomes including increased risk of cardiometabolic conditions, such as obesity (Du et al., 2026). These associations are correlational rather than causal and may partly reflect the health status of those who nap longer rather than the napping itself.

nap-spell.text: Beyond duration, the timing of a nap also shapes its effectiveness. Circadian rhythms are the body’s 24-hour clock for biological functions including body temperature, heart rate, and hormone secretion (Milner & Cote, 2009). These rhythms naturally produce a dip in alertness during the early-to-mid afternoon (Autumn et al., 2016; Shadab et al., 2026). Evidence suggests that the human body may be biologically inclined toward two sleep periods with a 24-hour cycle, with a primary nocturnal window and a secondary dip occurring between 13:00 and 15:00 (Autumn et al., 2016). Naps taken during this window tend to be more efficient, with shorter sleep latency and greater slow-wave sleep compared to naps taken later in the evening (Lavie & Weler, 1989). Naps outside of this window (particularly during the evening) risk increasing sleep inertia and interfering with nocturnal sleep (Naitoh, 1981). It is also worth noting that optimal timing may differ depending on an individual's level of fatigue: for those who are well-rested, a later afternoon nap may maximise benefits, whereas sleep-deprived individuals are likely to benefit from napping earlier in the day (Milner & Cote, 2009).

nap-spell.text: Strategies for Nap Initiation
nap-spell.html: Strategies for Nap Initiation

nap-spell.text: Sleep initiation is one of the most commonly reported difficulties among university students, with falling asleep identified as the predominant sleep complaint in this population (Lovato & Lack, 2010; Spyridonidis et al., 2025). Academic stress is a consistent contributor, with meta-analytic evidence indicating moderate associations between perceived stress and both poorer sleep quality and insomnia symptoms (Gardani et al., 2022). These effects appear to operate through overlapping pathways: heightened physiological arousal, stress-related rumination at bedtime, the irregular sleep schedules and late nights typical of student life. Importantly, these are not purely correlational observations; controlled laboratory evidence demonstrates that acute psychosocial stress can causally lengthen objectively measured sleep latency, both at night and during a nap (Goldberg et al., 2020).

nap-spell.text: For napping specifically, these mechanisms present a practical problem. Stress-induced cortisol elevation and sustained arousal reduce the likelihood of rapid sleep initiation within a short nap window (Ackermann et al., 2019). Several accessible strategies may help address this, including the consumption of kiwifruit approximately an hour before sleep. Kiwifruit contains several compounds associated with sleep regulation, including melatonin, serotonin-related properties, antioxidants, and folate (Hattori et al., 1995; Tsaluchidu et al., 2008; Nødtvedt et al., 2017). Intervention studies have linked its consumption to improvements in sleep continuity, quality, and mood in both athletes and healthy young adults (Doherty et al., 2023; Kanon et al., 2023). However, both studies examined nocturnal sleep rather than daytime napping, which limits the directness of their application here. Whether kiwifruit consumption before a nap would produce similar benefits, or alternatively prolong sleep duration in ways that increase sleep inertia, remain an open question. Research examining its specific effects on nap initiation and quality would be a valuable contribution to this area.

By directing attention toward present-moment experience, mindfulness may help reduce the cognitive and emotional activation that often delays sleep onset. The fact that this effect emerged from a single, scalable session suggests that mindfulness may be useful not because it eliminates stress entirely, but because it offers a practical means of disengaging from it at bedtime. Although the adolescent sample limits direct generalisation to university students, the low-cost and self-directed nature of the strategy makes it particularly well-suited to students managing academic stress independently.

More recent digital interventions point in the same direction, with Calm app users across both adult and undergraduate samples showing improvements in sleep quality, pre-sleep arousal, and stress (Huberty et al., 2021; Lew et al., 2025). Mindfulness is therefore best understood as a strategy that supports sleep onset indirectly, by reducing arousal and mental activation that interfere with sleep onset, rather than as a direct or guaranteed solution.

nap-spell.text: Writing a to-do list before bed may also help students fall asleep faster by reducing the cognitive arousal caused by unfinished tasks. Experimental evidence suggests that bedtime worry often centres on incomplete future responsibilities, and that externalising these onto paper may help offload them cognitively (Scullin et al., 2018). In a polysomnography study, participants who spent five minutes writing a list of upcoming tasks fell asleep significantly faster than those who wrote about already-completed tasks (d = 0.63, p = .02). Notably, the more specific the list, the shorter the sleep onset latency (r = -.39, p = .04). For students whose racing thoughts at bedtime often involve deadlines, unfinished studying, or next-day obligations, this is a low-effort strategy with meaningful empirical support.

nap-spell.text: Discussion
nap-spell.html: Discussion

nap-spell.text: Despite the scope of research reviewed here, several gaps remain in nap research. The cognitive benefits of napping are relatively well-documented, but its effects on mental health, particularly in young adults, are less understood. Much of the emotional and psychological literature focuses on older adults or young children, leaving university students somewhat underrepresented in this area. The sleep onset literature presents a similar problem: most intervention research targets nocturnal sleep, and studies examining how to facilitate nap initiation remains scarce. This is a meaningful gap given that stress-induced arousal may be most disruptive precisely in the short windows students have available to nap. It is also worth noting that many napping studies exclude participants who were unable to fall asleep during assigned nap opportunities, which inadvertently removes the people who may need the most help (Wofford et al., 2022).
